title: Brownout at 4:20 p.m.
note: Fictional unit and patients. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the charge nurse of a 15-station unit in Ormoc, Leyte. The utility power failed at 4:20 p.m. and the generator started. At 5:10 p.m. the technician reports that the promised fuel delivery has not come: the generator will run out within the hour. The utility says power will return “tonight.”

choices.text: No new connections; end sessions in an orderly way while the generator still runs (normal rinse-back with working alarms); call the backup fuel supplier and the attending nephrologist about patients cut short.
choices.feedback: A known end time lets you take patients off safely before the power goes.

choices.text: Wait for the utility to restore power tonight.
choices.feedback: “Tonight” is not a time. Waiting turns a planned take-off into a manual one.
choices.then: At 6:05 the generator stops with patients still on.

choices.text: Connect the evening shift on schedule; the utility should be back.
choices.feedback: Connecting new patients on a generator about to run dry exposes them to an emergency take-off.
choices.then: At 6:05 the generator stops with more patients connected.

n2.scene: The generator stops. Machines alarm on battery. Patients at Stations 3 and 11 are still connected.

choices.text: Walk the floor: check every patient’s airway, consciousness and access, and uncover the needle sites. Then decide with the physician-on-duty.

choices.feedback: Useful, but look at the patients before the equipment.

choices.text: Go to the generator room to see what happened.
choices.feedback: That is the technician’s job; your place is with the patients.
choices.then: A nurse calls you back to the floor.

n3.scene: The battery runs down; the blood pumps stop. Both circuits at Stations 3 and 11 look sound so far.

choices.text: One nurse at each station turns the hand crank and watches the venous drip chamber and line until the clamp is closed.
choices.feedback: Without power, the operator’s eyes replace the air detector: one staff member per patient.

choices.text: One nurse cranks both stations in turn, checking the lines between.
choices.feedback: Nobody watches the venous line while the other station is cranked; air can enter unseen.
choices.then: The charge nurse sends a second nurse to Station 11.

choices.text: Wait for power before returning the blood.
choices.feedback: Standing blood clots by the minute; the chance to return it is shrinking.
choices.then: You start the manual return a few minutes later.

n4.scene: At Station 11 the crank stiffens; the dialyzer shows dark streaks and the venous pressure rises. The circuit is clotting.

choices.text: Stop cranking, clamp and cut: do not force a clotted circuit back. Record the blood not returned and tell the attending nephrologist.
choices.feedback: Clotted blood is not forced back. The nephrologist decides the next session and any blood count check.

choices.text: Crank harder to push the blood through.
choices.feedback: Forcing a clotting circuit can send clots or rupture the circuit.
choices.then: The physician-on-duty stops you; the circuit is clamped.

end.title: 6:40 p.m.
end.text: Both patients are off. Station 3’s blood was returned by hand; Station 11’s was not. Times, methods and volumes are recorded, and the nephrologist has set their next sessions.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • A known end time is a gift: take patients off in order while the power still runs.
  • Without power, one staff member per patient watches the venous line, because the air detector may not work.
  • Never force a clotted circuit back; clamp, record and tell the nephrologist.
